new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress targets both the initial and the penultimate syllable, with the ranking depending on word length: disyllables initial (=penult); trisyllables normally initial/antepenult (some, esp. prefixed CV-prefix + heavy stem, penult); 4-syllable monomorphemes and reduplications primary initial + secondary penult; words of 5+ syllables (mostly polymorphemic) primary penult + secondary initial, typically dactyl+trochee. Author's headline generalisation: primary penult, secondary initial for words over three syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable when primary is penultimate (long words); on the third/penultimate syllable when primary is initial (4-syllable monomorphemes); trisyllables like murdura may carry secondary stress on the final syllable; monosyllabic postpositions after disyllabic hosts often add word-final secondary stress; in 6-syllable reduplications the initial syllable of the reduplicated portion retains stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Some trisyllables (often prefixed, open short first syllable + closed/long second syllable) take penult stress, with variation e.g. 'mung,gaya ~ mung'gaya; verbal words 'more complex' and not fully described; clitic -wurru and disyllabic nominal suffixes/postpositions behave as separate phonological words (stress on their first syllable); monosyllabic 3rd-person oblique -ngu not always stressed; a final vowel+glide-initial suffix diphthong is not stressed; fn. 21: stress judged by force/loudness, vowel lengthening used for emphasis, relation between vowel length and stress 'needs further investigation'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in isolated/citation forms of nominals and some inflected verbs (author notes verbs are rarely uttered in isolation and harder to test); impressionistic (auditory loudness), not instrumental. Variety: Wunambal proper, mainly Northern five-class dialect with some Southern-dialect speakers, recorded 1990s at Mowanjum/Derby/Kalumburu.
new_statements.identity_note: Carr 2000 describes Wunambal proper (glottocode wuna1249), mainly the Northern five-noun-class variety, with data also from Southern (three-class) Wunambal speakers at Mowanjum/Derby and Kalumburu (thesis 1.6.1, p.16). It is not a description of Gunin/Kwini (kwin1241) or Gamberre, which Glottolog treats as separate Wunambalic languages; McGregor 1993 (LINCOM) covers Kwini, not wuna1249.

sources.note: Dedicated section 2.4 Stress (pp. 61-63, fn. 21 p. 65): in words of more than 3 syllables primary stress normally penultimate with secondary stress on the first syllable; disyllables initial; trisyllables normally initial (antepenult), some penult; 4-syllable monomorphemic/reduplicated words primary on first, secondary on penult; 5-syllable words penult primary + initial secondary (dactyl+trochee); clitic -wurru and disyllabic suffixes/postpositions behave as phonological words attracting stress on their first syllable; stress judged by loudness, relation to vowel length left open.

sources.note: Ch. 1 'Phonological principles' (pp. 7-17) has no stress/accent subsection; only scattered remarks (e.g. 'one of the very rare accents on a final syllable', 'the fixity of the stress is noticeable also, even if it has to fall four syllables back from the end' re Worora, stress-conditioned allomorphy of *wu/*awu 'when the stress fell on the a: Wunambal'). No statement of where Wunambal word stress falls.
